summary: This document described a trivial convention for using HTTP to resolve Uniform Resource Names, as a mechanism the URN working group was considering alongside NAPTR. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2169 shows how a program can ask a web server to look up a URN, a name that identifies a resource without saying where it lives. The trick is that the request is an ordinary HTTP GET to a path such as /uri-res/N2L, so a server that already runs CGI scripts can answer it with very little new code.

subtitle: A small convention that lets an ordinary HTTP server answer URN resolution requests.

tldr.problem: A client that holds a URN needs to reach a database that knows about the named resource, and the NAPTR record only names the resolution protocol and services, not how to talk to them.
tldr.mechanism: THTTP encodes every resolution request as an ordinary HTTP GET under the path prefix /uri-res/, with the service name and the URN in the request, so any existing HTTP server can answer with a CGI script.
tldr.outcome: The RFC also sketches the text/uri-list format for returning lists of URIs and gives a short sample CGI script. It was published as an Experimental protocol and is Historic today, with no replacement RFC listed.

today: RFC 2169 is Historic, so it is no longer a current standards document, and the unit metadata lists no replacement RFC for it. The document was published in June 1997 as an Experimental protocol, at a time when the URN Working Group was considering the NAPTR proposal and THTTP was one of the resolution protocols a NAPTR record could name.

sections.title: Why a Trivial HTTP Convention
sections.content:
The Uniform Resource Names Working Group was formed to specify persistent, location-independent names for network accessible resources, and resolution mechanisms to retrieve the resources given such a name. One candidate mechanism was the NAPTR proposal, which defines a new DNS resource record that a client can use to discover a resolver for a URN. A resolver is a database that can provide information about the resource identified by a URN, such as the resource's location, a bibliographic description, or even the resource itself.

The NAPTR record has a field that names the resolution protocol the resolver speaks and the resolution services it offers, but it does not specify the protocol itself. The RFC names five resolution protocols mentioned in the NAPTR specification: Z3950, THTTP, RCDS, HDL and RWHOIS, with the list expected to grow over time. It also lists services such as N2L, given a URN and return a URL, and N2R, given a URN and return the named resource.

This document specifies THTTP, Trivial HTTP: a simple convention for encoding resolution service requests and responses as HTTP 1.0 or 1.1 requests and responses. Its primary goal is to be simple to implement, so that existing HTTP servers may easily add support for URN resolution, and the authors expect the databases used by early resolvers to remain useful when more sophisticated resolution protocols arrive later. The name THTTP is used rather than HTTP to leave that name free, because one protocol they expect to be developed is an extension of HTTP with new methods for the resolution services.

The reader is assumed to be familiar with the HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1 specifications, and implementors are expected to be familiar with CGI scripts or server-specific interfaces for database lookups.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN names a resource without giving its address. To fetch it, a client has to find a database that knows the resource and ask it a question. RFC 2169 makes that conversation ordinary HTTP so that any web server can take part with little extra work.

sections.title: The Request and Response Shape
sections.content:
The convention is one line. A resolution request is an HTTP GET whose path names the service and whose query string holds the URI being resolved:

GET /uri-res/<service>?<uri> HTTP/1.0

So a client that wants a URL for the URN urn:foo:12345-54321 sends GET /uri-res/N2L?urn:foo:12345-54321 HTTP/1.0. The same request can be written as HTTP/1.1, in which case it also carries a Host header. Responses follow standard HTTP practice: status codes such as 200 for OK or 404 for Not Found shall be returned, and the normal rules for deciding cachability and negotiating formats apply.

The server side is meant to be easy. A CGI script sees the incoming URI in the QUERY_STRING environment variable, with any percent-encoded characters still percent-encoded. The script can take the URN, look it up in a database and return the requested information.

The RFC flags one rule that implementors must respect. The URN syntax document discusses lexical equivalence and requires that resolvers return identical results for URNs that are lexically equivalent, so these two requests MUST return identical results:

GET /uri-res/N2L?urn:cid:foo@huh.com HTTP/1.0
GET /uri-res/N2L?URN:CID:foo@huh.com HTTP/1.0

Appendix B of the RFC gives a short Perl CGI script for the N2L service. It assumes a DBM database of URN to URL mappings, lowercases the namespace ID before the lookup, and prints a Location header. The RFC is clear that the script is a courtesy and does not specify standard behaviour: it neither processes incoming Accept headers nor generates status codes.
sections.plainLanguage: The request is a normal HTTP GET to a path that names the service, with the name being looked up after the question mark. The server hands that name to a script, the script looks it up in a database and answers. The RFC also insists that two spellings of the same URN must give the same answer.

sections.title: The Resolution Services
sections.content:
Each service is requested in the same way and differs only in what comes back. For N2L, a URN to URL, the URL MUST be returned in a Location header, and a successful lookup SHOULD return a 30X status line: 303 for HTTP/1.1 clients, and 302 for Moved temporarily for HTTP/1.0 clients unless the resolver has reasons to use 301 or 304 instead. Access controls may apply to any resolution service, so 401 and 403 are legal responses, and the server may add a body explaining the refusal and the price of obtaining the URL.

N2Ls returns a list of zero or more URLs. The media type may be negotiated with standard HTTP mechanisms, but the resolver must support at least text/uri-list, which suits machine processing. If the client asked for text/html, the result should be a valid HTML document containing a list of links.

N2R returns the resource itself using standard HTTP mechanisms, and the client may use the Accept header to ask for a preferred media type. N2Rs returns several instances of the same resource, for example a GIF version and a JPEG version of an image, as a multipart/alternative message with the versions in separate body parts; if there is only one version, it may be returned without that wrapper. The judgement about which resources count as the same rests with the naming authority that issued the URN.

N2C returns a description of the resource rather than the resource, for example a bibliographic citation, a digital signature or a revision history. The RFC does not specify what that description contains, so the format must be communicated in the ContentType header and the Accept header SHOULD be honoured. N2Ns returns the URNs that are believed to identify the same resource as the input URN. Some of those equivalences are transitory, as in a weather map that is current now and dated later, so the standard HTTP mechanisms for communicating cachability MUST be honoured.

The remaining services start from a URL instead of a URN. L2Ns returns a list of any URNs known to be assigned to the resource at that URL, L2Ls returns a list of all URLs known to be associated with that resource, and L2C returns a description of the resource, as for N2C.
sections.plainLanguage: Ten small services share the same request form and differ in the answer. Some return a single web address, some return a list of addresses, some return the resource itself, and some return a description of it rather than the thing itself.

sections.title: The text/uri-list Media Type
sections.content:
Several of the services, including N2Ls, N2Ns, L2Ns and L2Ls, answer with a list of URIs. Appendix A defines the text/uri-list media type to give those lists a simple format that programs can process automatically. The RFC notes that the appendix will be augmented or replaced once the media type has been registered.

The format has three rules. Lines beginning with the hash character are comment lines and are ignored, although a hash only introduces a comment when it is the first character on a line, since the character may also appear inside a URI. The remaining non-comment lines MUST be URIs, URNs or URLs, encoded according to the URI specification, and each URI appears on one and only one line. As for all text/* formats, lines are terminated with a CR LF pair, though clients should be liberal in accepting lines with only one of those characters.

Where one URI has been mapped to a list of URIs, as in an N2Ls answer, the first line SHOULD be a comment giving the original URI. The RFC prints an example of this, with the original URN as the comment and three addresses below it.
sections.plainLanguage: When a resolver returns a list of addresses, it returns them one per line, and any line starting with a hash sign is a comment that programs skip. This keeps the answer easy to read for a program and still readable for a person.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Communications with a resolver may be of a sensitive nature. Some resolvers hold information that should only be released to authorized users, so the answers to a resolution request can themselves be worth protecting.

The RFC also warns that results from resolvers may be the target of spoofing, especially once electronic commerce transactions are common and there is money to be made by directing users to pirate repositories rather than repositories which pay royalties to rightsholders. Resolution requests may be of interest to traffic analysts, and the requests may also be subject to spoofing.

The answer it gives is that the requests and responses in this draft are amenable to encoding, signing and authentication in the manner of any other HTTP traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A resolver may hold information that only some users should see, and its answers can be forged to send people to the wrong place. The RFC's answer is that because the exchange is ordinary HTTP, the same encoding, signing and authentication methods can be applied to it.

viz.caption: THE RESOLUTION SERVICES AND WHAT EACH RETURNS

items.label: URN to URL
items.desc: Returns one URL in a Location header, with a 30X status line.

items.label: URN to URLs
items.desc: Returns a list of zero or more URLs, at least as text/uri-list.

items.label: URN to Resource
items.desc: Returns the resource itself using standard HTTP mechanisms.

items.label: URN to Resources
items.desc: Returns several versions of the resource in a multipart/alternative message.

items.label: URN to URC
items.desc: Returns a description of the resource, such as a citation or a revision history.

items.label: URN to URNs
items.desc: Returns a list of URNs believed to identify the same resource.

items.label: URL to URNs
items.desc: Returns a list of URNs known to be assigned to the resource at that URL.

items.label: URL to URLs
items.desc: Returns a list of all URLs known to be associated with the resource.

items.label: URL to URC
items.desc: Returns a description of the resource at that URL, as for N2C.
